cues.text: Heir to a Warrior's Ambition
Born on March 9, 1568, in the castle of Castiglione delle Stiviere, Aloysius was the eldest son of Ferrante Gonzaga, Marquis of Castiglione.
Ferrante intended his firstborn for a distinguished military career and, when Aloysius was only eight years old, placed him in the court of Francesco de' Medici in Florence.
Two further years at the ducal court of Mantua followed.
Then, in 1581, Aloysius accompanied his father to Spain, where both brothers became pages to Don Diego, son of King Philip II.
This education in worldly ambition was one his father clearly hoped he would embrace.
A Vow Made in Childhood
Aloysius's own heart, however, had already turned elsewhere.
At Brescia, aged only twelve, he came under the spiritual direction of St. Charles Borromeo , who gave him his First Communion.

By nine, he had already resolved on a life of religious consecration, privately vowing himself to perpetual chastity—a resolve he kept with discipline, contemporaries noted, unusual even among far older religious.
Delicate health, the result of a kidney ailment, kept him for a time from the ordinary pursuits of court life, and he turned instead to prayer and to reading the lives of the saints.
He would later recall that even amid the pageantry of a royal court, he found himself drawn more to solitary prayer than to the amusements expected of a nobleman's son.
Renouncing a Marquisate
While in Spain, Aloysius distinguished himself in a public examination in both philosophy and theology at the University of Alcalá.
His growing conviction that he was called to the Society of Jesus set him on a collision course with his father's plans.
Only after years of difficulty did he secure his father's reluctant consent.
On November 2, 1585, he formally renounced his inheritance and title in favor of his younger brother.
Because Castiglione was a fief of the Empire, the renunciation required the emperor's own approval before taking legal effect.
Entering the Society of Jesus

Aloysius entered the Jesuit novitiate at Rome shortly afterward and made his religious vows on November 25, 1587, beginning theological studies under respected masters including Fathers Gabriel Vasquez and Juan Azor.
Those who knew him during these years described a young religious of unusual interior recollection.
He kept his eyes persistently downcast in company and gave himself with total seriousness to every ordinary duty of formation.
This total gift of self had, by this point, cost him a marquisate and a court career without a trace of visible regret.
Death Amid Plague
In 1591, in his fourth year of theology, famine and pestilence broke out across Italy.
Though his own health remained delicate, Aloysius threw himself into caring for the sick in Rome's hospitals, carrying the dying in his own arms when necessary.
He fell seriously ill himself on March 3 of that year.
After several months of decline, he died on June 21, 1591, not yet twenty-three years old.
His death closed, in its final act, the very pattern of self-forgetful service his whole short life had already traced.
Companions later testified that he nursed patients others feared to approach, judging the risk to his own fragile health a small price for the corporal work of mercy directly in front of him.
Legacy
Aloysius was beatified in 1605 by Pope Paul V and canonized in 1726 by Pope Benedict XIII, who three years later named him patron of youth, an honor Pope Pius XI confirmed and extended in 1926.
His relics rest today in the church of St. Ignatius in Rome, beneath a magnificent urn of lapis lazuli.
For every young person who has felt the pull between others’ ambitions and a quieter, more demanding call of their own, Aloysius Gonzaga remains a companion.
He proves that a total gift of self, offered while still young, loses nothing by being offered early.
